theme: The Temple sermon; false security condemned
readingInstruction: Read Jeremiah 7:1-9:26. Jeremiah stands in the gate of the temple and preaches the most dangerous sermon of his life. Read it as a warning to people who think that being near the right building makes them safe.
settingTheScene: This is the Temple Sermon, delivered early in the reign of Jehoiakim, around 609 BC (see Jeremiah 26). The people believed that Jerusalem could never fall because the temple of the LORD was there. After the Assyrian army was destroyed in Hezekiah’s day, that belief hardened into superstition. Jeremiah tells them it is a lie. Chapters 8 and 9 add the prophet’s tears over the nation.
observation: “Do not trust in these deceptive words: This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD” (7:4).
“If you truly amend your ways and your deeds… if you do not oppress the sojourner, the fatherless, or the widow” (7:5-6).
“Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes?” (7:11).
“Go now to my place that was in Shiloh… and see what I did to it” (7:12).
“For in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, I did not speak to your fathers… concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices. But this command I gave them: Obey my voice” (7:22-23).
“Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there?” (8:22).
“Oh that my head were a spring of water, and my eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night” (9:1).
“Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom… but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me” (9:23-24).
interpretation:
The sermon begins with a trap. The people repeat a slogan: “The temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD.” They treat the building as a charm. Jeremiah says that if they are going to live there, they must act justly: no oppression of the foreigner, the orphan, or the widow, no shedding of innocent blood, no following other gods. They steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely, and then come into the temple and say, “We are delivered!” That is, they think the temple frees them to keep doing evil.

God’s reply is that they have turned his house into “a den of robbers.” A den is where robbers hide after their crimes. Jesus quotes this very line when he clears the temple. Then God points to Shiloh, where the tabernacle once stood, and which had been destroyed. If he allowed that, he can allow this.

Verses 21 to 23 are a shock. God says that when he brought them out of Egypt, his main command was not about sacrifices but about obedience. The sacrifices were meant to express the relationship, not replace it.

Chapter 8 contains one of the most poignant questions in the Bible: “Is there no balm in Gilead?” Gilead was known for healing ointment. The prophet asks why his people are not healed, since there is a physician. The answer is that they will not be healed. And chapter 9 shows the prophet weeping. “Oh that my head were a spring of water.” He is the true intercessor.

The chapter ends with a great statement of what matters: let no one boast in wisdom, might, or riches, but in knowing the LORD, “who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness.”
connection: Jesus quoted Jeremiah 7:11 when he cleansed the temple (Mark 11:17), and then said that not one stone would be left on another (Mark 13:2). Paul quotes Jeremiah 9:24 in 1 Corinthians 1:31 and 2 Corinthians 10:17. Jesus is the true physician (Mark 2:17). Acts 7:48 reminds us that the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands. 1 Corinthians 3:16 says that the believers are God’s temple.
application:
Ask whether any place, ritual, or tradition has become a “temple of the LORD” slogan for you.

Look at how you treat the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow. Is there something to change?

Memorize Jeremiah 9:23-24 and ask what you are tempted to boast in.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to keep you from trusting deceptive words.
Ask him not to let you hide in his house while sin remains.
Ask him to make you just and merciful toward the weak.
